steps.tx: **Screen** for **primary** aldosteronism in resistant hypertension, hypertension with spontaneous or diuretic-induced hypokalemia, an adrenal incidentaloma with hypertension, early-onset hypertension, or a family history of early hypertension or stroke. Many patients are normokalaemic, so a normal potassium does not exclude the disease. The drawing shows a canary yellow cortical adenoma driving sodium retention and potassium loss, which is why the potassium can be low, but a normal potassium is still compatible.

vis.alt: Drawing of a canary yellow adenoma on the adrenal cortex and a collecting duct reabsorbing sodium and excreting potassium.
vis.caption: The drawing shows a canary yellow cortical adenoma and a collecting duct taking up sodium and losing potassium. It does not show the aldosterone to renin ratio (StewardMD).

steps.tx: The **screening test** is the plasma aldosterone concentration divided by plasma renin. A commonly used positive screen is a ratio above 30 when aldosterone is measured in ng/dL and renin in ng/mL/h, together with an aldosterone above 10 ng/dL. The laboratory's own cutoff and units must be used. A ratio without the units is not an answer, because a direct renin concentration uses a different number from plasma renin activity.

steps.tx: **Stop spironolactone** and eplerenone for 4 to 6 weeks before the ratio, because they raise renin and can falsely normalise the screen. A beta blocker can suppress renin and falsely raise the ratio, so an abnormal result on a beta blocker still needs confirmation. Do not stop every antihypertensive for weeks in a patient with dangerous pressure. The mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are the drugs that most reliably wreck the screen.

points: They raise renin and hide the disease

right.title: Interpret with care

An abnormal result still needs confirmation

steps.tx: **Confirm** with a suppression test unless spontaneous hypokalaemia, undetectable renin, and a plasma aldosterone above 20 ng/dL already make the diagnosis obvious. After intravenous saline, failure of aldosterone to fall below 10 ng/dL supports primary aldosteronism. Saline loading is avoided in uncontrolled hypertension or heart failure. A patient who is already in pulmonary oedema does not need a saline infusion to prove the diagnosis.

steps.tx: A **unilateral aldosterone**-producing adenoma, Conn syndrome, is treated by laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Bilateral idiopathic hyperplasia is treated with a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist. Spironolactone causes gynecomastia, and eplerenone is the alternative. The yellow nodule on the drawing is the adenoma you can remove. Hyperplasia is not a nodule you should chase with an operation on both glands.

steps.tx: **Adrenal vein** sampling is recommended before surgery in most patients who want an operation. It can be omitted in a patient younger than 35 years with marked aldosterone excess, spontaneous hypokalaemia, and a clear unilateral adenoma with a normal contralateral gland on imaging. Imaging cannot tell a nonfunctioning adenoma from an aldosterone-producing one in an older adult. Do not book the theatre from the CT alone.

steps.tx: **Familial hyperaldosteronism** type I, glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism, is a chimeric CYP11B1/CYP11B2 gene. Aldosterone is under ACTH control, so low-dose dexamethasone suppresses it, and family members are screened. It presents with early hypertension and haemorrhagic stroke. The drawing shows the chimeric gene, ACTH driving ectopic aldosterone synthase, and a family history of early haemorrhagic stroke.

steps.tx: Do not **start** a **workup** for primary aldosteronism by removing an incidental adrenal nodule. Imaging cannot tell a nonfunctioning adenoma from an aldosterone-producing one. Biochemistry and, when needed, adrenal vein sampling come first. A normal potassium is not a reason to skip the ratio when the blood pressure is resistant. Screen, confirm, then decide who goes to sampling, and only then decide who goes to theatre.
